# In Praise of Maintenance

The word "maintain" comes from the Latin *manu tenere*: to hold in the hand. I find this etymology moving in a way that surprises me. Before maintenance was a budget line or a chore, it was a gesture — the act of keeping something from falling by holding onto it. Everything that persists in this world persists because something or someone holds it. The bridge is held by inspectors and painters. The language is held by speakers. The garden is held by the gardener, and the moment she lets go, the wilderness begins taking it back, politely at first, then with increasing confidence.

We live in a culture obsessed with creation and dismissive of upkeep. We celebrate founders, inventors, disruptors, visionaries. We give awards for the new building, never for the fifty years of keeping it standing. And yet, if you tally the hours of human effort expended on this planet in any given week, the overwhelming majority of them go toward maintenance: cleaning, fixing, patching, mending, restocking, recalibrating, sweeping, oiling, debugging, dusting, reassuring. The world is not primarily a made thing. It is a *kept* thing. Creation happens once; maintenance happens forever after, or the creation ceases to exist. This essay is an attempt to look directly at the work we have trained ourselves not to see.

---

## The Manifesto

In 1969, an artist named Mierle Laderman Ukeles, recently a mother and exhausted by the endless cycle of care work that motherhood demanded, sat down and wrote the "Manifesto for Maintenance Art." In it she drew a distinction between what she called the death instinct and the life instinct. The death instinct, she said, drives toward separation, individuality, the new, the avant-garde — *following one's own path to death, do your own thing, dynamic change*. The life instinct drives toward unification, the perpetuation of species, survival systems, equilibrium. And then she asked a devastating question: after the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?

Ukeles spent the next decades making art out of this question. Her most famous work, *Touch Sanitation*, took eleven months, during which she traveled to every sanitation district in New York City and shook hands with roughly 8,500 sanitation workers, saying to each one: "Thank you for keeping New York City alive." Some of them wept. Nobody had ever said it before. They were used to being seen as the thing adjacent to garbage rather than as the system that stands between a city of millions and its own filth — which is to say, between a city and plague, between a city and collapse.

What Ukeles understood is that the invisibility of maintenance is not an accident. It is structural. Maintenance, done well, produces nothing visible. Its product is the *absence* of catastrophe, the *non-occurrence* of decay, and absence is hard to celebrate. You cannot photograph the bridge not collapsing. The better a maintainer does their job, the less evidence exists that they did anything at all. We notice the janitor only when the floor is dirty, the IT department only when the server is down, the body's immune system only when it fails. Maintenance is a performance whose success is measured by its own disappearance.

---

## The Shrine That Is Always New and Always Ancient

At Ise, in Japan, there is a Shinto shrine that has stood for around 1,300 years and is also, at any given moment, no more than two decades old. Every twenty years, in a ritual called Shikinen Sengū, the shrine is completely rebuilt on an adjacent plot, using traditional joinery, cypress wood, and techniques passed down across more than sixty rebuilding cycles. The old structure is dismantled. The new one, identical, takes its place. Then the cycle begins again.

Western conservation has often found this baffling, even scandalous. Where is the *authentic* shrine? Surely a building rebuilt sixty times is a replica, not an original? But this confusion reveals an assumption worth questioning: that the essence of a thing lives in its material substance rather than in its form, its function, its continuity of practice. The shrine at Ise has decided that what must be preserved is not the wood but the *knowledge* — the carpentry, the rituals, the precise angle of every joint. The twenty-year cycle is roughly the span of a working generation; it ensures that master builders always train apprentices on a real rebuilding, that the knowledge never has to survive a gap. The building is mortal so that the building-knowledge can be immortal.

This is the Ship of Theseus paradox resolved not as a puzzle but as a practice. The ancient question asks: if you replace every plank of a ship one by one, is it still the same ship? Ise answers: that's the wrong question. The ship was never the planks. The ship is the pattern, and the pattern persists only through continuous renewal. Identity, on this view, is not a substance but an activity — something you *do* rather than something you *have*.

And here is the part that gets me: this is also true of you. The cells of your body are continuously replaced; the atoms cycle through; the stomach lining renews itself in days, the skeleton over years. You are not the matter you were a decade ago. You are a standing wave, a pattern that maintains itself through perpetual material turnover, a shrine rebuilt continuously on the same sacred ground. To be alive is to be a maintenance project that has not yet been abandoned.

---

## Painting the Forth Bridge

In Britain, "painting the Forth Bridge" used to be shorthand for an endless task. The great cantilever railway bridge over the Firth of Forth, completed in 1890, was said to require such constant repainting that by the time the crews finished at one end, the other end needed starting again. The phrase entered the language as a gentle joke about futility — Sisyphus with a paintbrush, in Scottish weather.

I have always thought the joke gets it backwards. There is nothing futile about painting the Forth Bridge. The futility would be *not* painting it. The bridge sits in salt air; steel in salt air wants, with the full patience of chemistry, to become rust. The Second Law of Thermodynamics is the most undefeated force in the universe: left alone, everything drifts toward disorder, and the drift never sleeps, never takes a holiday, never gets discouraged. Every ordered thing in existence — every bridge, every cell, every institution, every relationship, every database — is a temporary local rebellion against entropy, and the rebellion must be continuously funded or it ends.

Seen this way, the painters of the Forth Bridge were not engaged in a comic exercise in futility. They were engaged in the fundamental human project: holding a piece of order against the universal slide. The bridge has carried trains for over 130 years. That is not a building's lifespan; that is a *relationship's* lifespan — five generations of maintainers handing a bridge to one another like a family heirloom that happens to weigh 50,000 tons. (In 2011, engineers finished applying a modern coating expected to last twenty-five years, and the endless painting finally paused. I confess I found the news faintly melancholy, the way one feels when a long argument between old friends finally gets settled.)

---

## The Cables and the Code

Consider, for a moment, the physical substrate of the internet. We talk about "the cloud" as if data lived in the sky, but in truth nearly all intercontinental data travels through cables on the ocean floor — bundles of glass fibers, often no thicker than a garden hose, lying in the dark across abyssal plains. And these cables break. Anchors snag them. Fishing trawlers cut them. Undersea landslides snap them. Occasionally a shark bites one, which feels like nature's editorial comment.

When a cable breaks, a repair ship goes out. Crews drag grapnels across the seafloor to hook the broken cable, haul each severed end to the surface — sometimes from depths of several kilometers — and splice the hair-thin glass fibers back together in a clean room aboard the ship, work of almost surgical delicacy performed on a vessel rolling in open ocean. Then they lower the mended cable back into the dark and sail on. These ships and crews wait on standby in ports around the world, the way fire departments wait, because the breaks are not hypothetical; they are constant. Somewhere right now, almost certainly, someone is splicing the internet back together with their hands. Your video call crosses an ocean because of them, and you will never learn their names.

Software tells the same story at a different altitude. The popular image of programming is invention — the genius building the new thing in a garage. The reality is that the great majority of software engineering effort goes into maintaining systems that already exist: patching vulnerabilities, updating dependencies, fixing the bug that only appears on the last day of months with thirty-one days. Enormous portions of the world's financial infrastructure still run on COBOL, a language from 1959, kept alive by a dwindling priesthood of programmers, some lured out of retirement when crises hit. We call old code "legacy" with a sneer, but a legacy is, literally, an inheritance — something valuable enough that someone bothered to pass it down. Code becomes legacy code by *succeeding*: by mattering enough that it cannot be allowed to die.

The historians Lee Vinsel and Andrew Russell have argued that our culture suffers from an "innovation delusion" — a fixation on novelty that starves the maintenance on which everything actually depends. We fund the ribbon-cutting and defer the repairs, and the deferred repairs accumulate quietly until a bridge falls or a water system poisons a city. Innovation, they point out, is a moment; maintenance is the rest of the lifespan. A technology spends perhaps one percent of its existence being invented and ninety-nine percent being kept alive. Our attention is allocated in precisely inverse proportion.

---

## The Golden Repair

There is a Japanese practice called kintsugi: when a ceramic bowl breaks, rather than discarding it or repairing it invisibly, the cracks are mended with lacquer dusted with gold. The repair is not hidden. It is illuminated. The bowl's history of damage becomes the most beautiful thing about it, a network of bright veins announcing: *this object broke, and someone judged it worth mending.*

I think kintsugi endures as an idea — it has become almost a cliché of self-help, and I want to rescue it from that — because it inverts our deepest assumption about damage. We tend to believe that a thing's value peaks at the moment of manufacture and declines with every scratch. Kintsugi proposes the opposite: that the repaired object is *more* valuable than the pristine one, because the pristine object is merely well-made, while the repaired object is *loved*. Repair is the proof. Nobody mends what they don't care about. The golden seam is a receipt for affection.

The same impulse animates the "visible mending" movement among menders of clothes — darning a sweater's elbow in deliberately contrasting thread, patching jeans with bright sashiko stitching, turning the repair into ornament. It is a small act of resistance against an economy built on disposal, an economy that has made replacement cheaper than repair and trained us to experience breakage as a shopping opportunity. Every visible mend says: this thing has a history, and its history continues. To throw away a mendable thing is to break a sentence off mid-

---

## What Love Actually Looks Like

I want to end somewhere more intimate, because I think maintenance is, finally, not really about bridges or cables or bowls. It is about the structure of care itself.

When people describe love, they reach for the language of creation and peak experience: falling in love, the spark, the lightning strike. But anyone who has loved anything for a long time knows that love's actual texture is maintenance. It is the friendship sustained by the regular call that is never urgent and never skipped. It is the marriage upheld by ten thousand small repairs — the apology offered, the irritation released, the conversation had again because it needed having again. It is the parent making the same breakfast the same way because the sameness *is* the message. It is showing up at the bedside, the recital, the funeral. None of these acts is impressive in isolation. Like all maintenance, they produce nothing visible; they produce the non-occurrence of drift, the absence of estrangement. You cannot photograph a friendship not dissolving.

We dishonor this work when we treat it as the boring part of life — the stuff between the highlights. The highlights are not the life. The maintenance is the life. A garden is not the photograph of the garden in June; it is the weeding in March and the watering in August. A self is not the resume; it is the daily practice that keeps the skills and decencies from rusting. Even meaning is a maintained thing: convictions left unexamined go slack, gratitude unexercised atrophies, attention unguarded drifts to whatever glows loudest. The inner life needs its painters on the bridge too.

There is a sentence I keep returning to, a plain fact that becomes stranger the longer you look at it: everything you love is being held. The book survives because librarians fought the mold and the silverfish. The recipe survives because someone made it again. The language you think in survives because millions of mouths keep it warm. The road, the vaccine cold chain, the power grid, the orchard, the friendship, the democracy — none of it is self-sustaining; all of it is held, every day, by hands mostly unthanked, in work mostly unseen. The world is not a possession we inherited. It is a fire that has been carefully banked and passed along, person to person, for ten thousand years, by people who understood that their real job was not to make the flame but to keep it from going out.

So here is my small proposal, my golden seam at the end of this essay: notice the maintainers. Thank the person mopping the floor. Fix the thing instead of replacing it, at least once, just to remember what it feels like. Make the call that keeps the friendship painted against the salt air. And when you do the unglamorous work of keeping something alive — a skill, a garden, a person's trust, your own battered hope — do it without embarrassment, knowing you have joined the oldest and most honorable guild there is.

After the revolution, somebody picks up the garbage on Monday morning. That somebody is not the footnote to civilization.

That somebody is civilization.
